about: Skills tool: water potential calculations. Solver and generator: ApBioProblems, kind wp (mode cell or zero). R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K) and T = °C + 273, as on the formula sheet.
intro: Calculate solute potential and water potential, and use them to say which way water moves. To watch the same ideas play out, try the osmosis simulator.
howItWorksTitle: The formulas, and how answers are checked
howItWorks:
ψ = ψs + ψp

ψs = −iCRT

  • i is the number of particles each unit of solute makes in water: 1 for sucrose and glucose, 2 for NaCl (we assume it splits completely), 3 for CaCl₂.
  • C is the molar concentration (mol/L); R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K); T is the temperature in kelvins: °C + 273.
  • A solution in an open container has pressure potential ψp = 0, so its ψ = ψs. Pure water at atmospheric pressure has ψ = 0.
  • Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential.
  • Answers in bar count when within 0.01 bar or 1%, whichever is larger (using 273.15 K instead of 273 K also counts).

contexts.text: A plant cell’s sap has the same solute potential as {cellC} M {cellSolute}, and its turgor pressure (ψp) is {psiP} bar. The cell is placed in an open beaker of {solC} M {solSolute} at {T} °C.
Potato cores left in a series of sucrose solutions at {T} °C neither gained nor lost mass in {C} M sucrose.

input.text: An onion cell’s sap has the solute potential of 0.40 M sucrose, and its turgor pressure is 2.0 bar. It is placed in an open beaker of 0.25 M NaCl at 20 °C.
A leaf cell’s sap has the solute potential of 0.50 M glucose, and its turgor pressure is 3.5 bar. It is placed in an open beaker of 0.20 M sucrose at 25 °C.
Sweet potato cores left in sucrose solutions at 22 °C neither gained nor lost mass in 0.35 M sucrose.
